title: How I Use AI as a Thought Partner
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton, a math education expert, presents a five-step framework for using AI as a genuine thought partner in instructional design rather than as a cognitive outsourcing machine or a simple formatter. He distinguishes two traps: the first is cognitive outsourcing (letting AI do the thinking while you copy and paste), and the second is under-using AI (doing all the thinking yourself and using AI only for layout). His framework occupies the productive middle: end every prompt with 'Before you build, ask me some clarifying questions'; invite the AI to be a critical collaborator that challenges your thinking; scrutinize the first output like a colleague's draft; iterate through multiple versions; and ask the AI what it learned from the collaboration at the end. Barton illustrates the framework with five concrete examples from his recent work designing sequences of positive and negative examples for teaching categorical concepts in mathematics, showing how AI pushed back on his proposed examples and improved the sequence. He also argues that voice input via tools like Wispr Flow frees working memory to focus on ideas rather than typing, and that the context-rich, discursive prompts enabled by dictation produce better AI outputs.
points: The two failure modes of AI use are symmetric: cognitive outsourcing (AI does the thinking, you copy/paste) and under-use (you do all the thinking, AI just formats)—and both are traps, though the first is far more serious because it atrophies pedagogical reasoning.

Ending every prompt with 'Before you build, ask me some clarifying questions' is the single easiest way to shift from passive execution to collaborative thinking, because it forces both you and the AI to clarify what you actually want before building anything.

The critical line that turns an AI from an order-taker into a peer is explicit permission to disagree: 'I don't want you to just accept every suggestion I make. I want you to challenge me with reasons when appropriate.' Without that line, the AI's default is to agree with you.

Iterating through multiple rounds of feedback is where the real cognitive work happens: the second version will be better than the first, but rarely finished, and most final resources require three or four rounds of specific, reasoned feedback.

Asking the AI 'What did you learn from this collaboration?' at the end—and saving those principles for the start of the next session—creates a compounding improvement loop across resources, and applying the same reflective question to yourself doubles the effect.
quotes: That is trap number one: cognitive outsourcing, to use Paul Kirschner's phrase. The AI does the thinking, you copy and paste, and your own pedagogical reasoning slowly atrophies.

The crucial line is the one in the middle: 'I don't want you to just accept every suggestion I make. I want you to challenge me with reasons when appropriate.' Without that, the AI's default is to agree with you. With it, you give the AI permission to behave like a peer.

The final resource often ends up better than what I would have produced on my own. Partly because I am drawing on the AI's expertise. But mostly because I am freed from the grunt work — the typing, the formatting, the layout — and that frees up working memory to notice things about the pedagogy I would have missed if I had been doing the whole job myself.

When I am typing, a chunk of my working memory is on the keyboard. When I am dictating, all of it is on the idea. I can chase a half-formed thought before it slips away. I can include the kind of throwaway context — 'what worries me here is…', 'and I think the reason is…' — that I would strip out if I were writing.

The more I read about how large language models work, the more I realise they are hungry for that kind of context. The flowery asides we filter out when typing turn out to be exactly what sharpens the output.
Save those principles. Paste them into the start of the next chat. The next resource will be better, quicker.
